questions.stem:
A 20-month-old girl has had fever to 39.4 C (102.9 F) for 5 days. She has injected bulbar conjunctivae that spare the area around the cornea, with no discharge; red, cracked, bleeding lips; a bright red tongue; a blanching rash over her trunk; and swollen hands with red palms sharply demarcated at the wrists. She is fussy but alert, and her blood pressure is normal for age.

[[labs 0]]

Which test should be obtained now, at presentation?
choices: Lumbar puncture with spinal fluid culture
Echocardiogram to assess the coronary arteries
Skin biopsy of the rash with immunohistochemistry
Rapid antigen test for influenza from the nose
Serum IgM antibody against parvovirus B19

explain.html: Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis of young children diagnosed clinically after at least 5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 features: bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, oral changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), a polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema and redness of the hands and feet), and unilateral cervical lymphadenitis. The workshop case shows the typical details: conjunctival injection with limbic sparing, palms and soles with a red-purple color sharply demarcated at the wrists and ankles, and labs with a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis, a high platelet count, low albumin, mildly raised transaminases, and white cells in the urine with no organisms. This girl has 5 days of fever and four features plus the same supportive labs. The danger is the heart: untreated, about 20% of children develop coronary artery abnormalities including aneurysms, so an echocardiogram at presentation sets a baseline and looks for myocarditis before IVIG and aspirin are given.

Workshop caseKey cluesDiagnosis

why: A lumbar puncture is not part of the standard workup here, and nothing points to meningitis.
Skin biopsy immunohistochemistry is one way to diagnose Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which brings a petechial rash after tick exposure.
Influenza testing addresses neither the mucocutaneous findings nor the coronary risk.
Parvovirus B19 gives a slapped-cheek rash, not conjunctival, oral, and extremity changes.
explain.takeaway: Kawasaki disease (5 days of fever plus 4 of 5 mucocutaneous criteria, sterile pyuria, thrombocytosis, low albumin) needs an echocardiogram at presentation because untreated disease causes coronary aneurysms.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize Kawasaki disease from its fever, mucocutaneous, and laboratory findings, and know the first test once it is suspected (Case #2)

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old girl on her menstrual period has had 2 days of fever, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, and muscle aches, and today she nearly fainted on standing. Blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg supine, pulse 160/min, and capillary refill 6 seconds. She has total body erythroderma most intense on the inner thighs, palms, and soles, injected conjunctivae, and enlarged tongue papillae. Platelets are 70,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (22 to 28). Her mother, who uses the same tampon brand, has never had a similar illness.

Which of the following best explains why adolescents and young adults are at higher risk than older adults for this illness?
choices: They have fewer T cells that can respond to superantigens
They are more often colonized by toxin-producing streptococci
They have not yet developed late complement components
They lack neutralizing antibody against the toxin
They have more P antigen expressed on their red cells

explain.html: Toxic shock syndrome is a diffuse inflammatory response driven by a superantigen toxin from Staphylococcus aureus (TSST-1) or group A streptococcus, causing fever, rash, hypotension, and multiorgan injury. The workshop case is the menstrual form: a 16-year-old on her period with fever, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, near-syncope, total body erythroderma most intense on the inner thighs, palms, and soles, injected conjunctivae, oral hyperemia, shock with slow capillary refill, low platelets, and a low bicarbonate. Whether a colonized person becomes ill depends on antibody: TSS is more likely in younger people who have no neutralizing antibody to the toxin their organism makes. Older adults have usually met the toxin before and carry antibody that neutralizes it, which is why the staphylococcal form clusters in ages 15 to 35 and why her mother, using the same tampons, has stayed well.
explain.table:
FeatureStaphylococcal TSSStreptococcal TSS
Typical settingMenstruation and tamponsSkin or joint infection, often after sore throat or a cut
ToxinTSST-1 (superantigen)Pyrogenic exotoxins A and B (superantigens)
BacteremiaLowCommon
AntibioticsAnti-staphylococcal plus a protein synthesis inhibitorAnti-streptococcal plus a protein synthesis inhibitor
Add-onSource removal (tampon)IVIG, surgical source control
why: Young people do not have fewer responsive T cells; the problem is that nothing neutralizes the toxin before it reaches them.
The menstrual, tampon-associated form is caused by Staphylococcus aureus, not streptococci.
Late complement components are present from infancy, and their deficiency predisposes to Neisseria, not toxic shock.
The P antigen is the parvovirus B19 receptor and plays no role in toxic shock.
explain.takeaway: Toxic shock syndrome is more likely in adolescents and young adults because they lack neutralizing antibody to TSST-1 or streptococcal superantigens; older adults usually carry it.

questions.stem:
A 10-month-old girl had 3 days of high fever, irritability, and decreased appetite with no cough, runny nose, or diarrhea. On the third day, the fever broke suddenly and a pink, discrete, blanching, nonitchy rash appeared on her trunk, spreading to the face, neck, and limbs over 2 days. She is fully immunized. She is now afebrile, well appearing, eating and drinking, and has palpable occipital nodes. Her buccal mucosa is normal.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Reassurance and supportive care
Serum measles IgM and airborne isolation
Blood culture and intravenous ceftriaxone
Echocardiogram and intravenous immunoglobulin
Throat culture and oral penicillin

explain.html: Roseola (exanthem subitum) from human herpesvirus 6 is a mild illness of infants, recognized by the order of events rather than by any test. The child has an abrupt high fever for about 3 days, sometimes with irritability or a febrile seizure, and then the fever breaks and a pink, discrete, blanching rash appears after the fever subsides, spreading from the trunk to the face, neck, and limbs. The workshop case is this exact story: a 10-month-old without cough, coryza, or diarrhea, fully immunized, well appearing and eating, with occipital nodes and a normal buccal mucosa. Roseola is a clinical diagnosis that resolves on its own, so reassurance and supportive care are appropriate. The key contrast is that in measles and most other viral exanthems the rash comes while the child is still febrile.

why: Measles is unlikely in an immunized infant with no cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, or Koplik spots, and its rash comes during fever.
A well, afebrile infant with a blanching rash does not need empiric treatment for meningococcal sepsis.
Kawasaki disease needs at least 5 days of fever and mucocutaneous findings this infant does not have.
Scarlet fever affects school-aged children with pharyngitis and a sandpaper rash.
explain.takeaway: Roseola (HHV-6) is a clinical diagnosis: an infant with about 3 days of high fever whose rash appears only after the fever breaks, needing only supportive care.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize roseola from the timing of fever and rash in a well infant (Case #1)

questions.stem:
An 11-month-old unvaccinated boy has had 5 days of fever to 40.4 C (104.8 F). On day 3 he developed a harsh cough and was treated with amoxicillin for presumed pneumonia without improvement. Today a morbilliform rash began on his head and spread to his trunk and limbs. He has red conjunctivae and is irritable. He attends a home daycare with three other infants, and his mother asks for how long he may have been spreading the illness.

This child was most contagious during which of the following periods?
choices: Only while the rash is visible on the trunk
From about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash
Only after the rash fades and the skin peels
For up to 6 weeks, through virus in the stool
Only during the 10 days before the cough began

explain.html: Measles is one of the most contagious infections: about 9 of 10 susceptible contacts develop disease, spread is airborne and by direct contact, and the incubation period is about 10 to 12 days. The illness begins with a prodrome of high fever with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, and the maculopapular rash follows days later, starting on the head and spreading downward. The workshop case shows how it gets missed: an unvaccinated 11-month-old's harsh cough on day 3 was treated as pneumonia, and the diagnosis became clear only when a morbilliform rash spread from the head on day 5. Patients are most contagious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash, so this child was shedding virus during the prodrome, before anyone suspected measles, and his unvaccinated daycare contacts are at risk.
why: Spread starts days before the rash, during the cough and fever, not only while the rash is visible.
Contagiousness falls after the rash, so recovery is not the main risk period.
Prolonged shedding in stool describes live oral polio vaccine virus, not measles.
The incubation period after exposure is not the contagious window; spread peaks around the rash.
explain.takeaway: Measles is most contagious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears, so spread begins during the cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis prodrome.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize measles in an unvaccinated infant and know when it is contagious (Case #11)

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old boy who moved to the US from Central America 8 months ago, with no vaccine records, has 3 days of fever to 39.9 C (103.8 F), myalgia, headache, and nausea. Red bumps appeared on the back of his neck and upper back on day 2. Today he has more than 500 lesions over his body, some papules, some fluid-filled vesicles, and some open and crusting, plus lesions on his conjunctiva and in his mouth. He appears ill.

Which drug is most appropriate for this patient?
choices: Penicillin
Doxycycline
Acyclovir
Azithromycin
Clindamycin

explain.html: Varicella is primary infection with varicella zoster virus, a DNA herpesvirus. After a short prodrome of fever and malaise, a vesicular rash begins centrally and spreads, and new crops keep appearing so that papules, vesicles, and crusted lesions are present at the same time. That mix of stages separates it from smallpox and mpox, where all lesions are in the same stage, and the workshop pairs them side by side for that reason. The workshop case is this patient: an adolescent recently arrived from Central America with high fever, myalgia, headache, and more than 500 lesions, some opened and leaking, plus conjunctival and oral lesions, and he looks ill. Older, unvaccinated patients with heavy or mucosal disease are ill enough to treat, and varicella zoster infections are treated with the antiviral acyclovir (or valacyclovir); antibacterial drugs have no effect on the virus.
why: Penicillin treats group A streptococcal infection such as scarlet fever and has no activity against a virus.
Doxycycline treats rickettsial infection such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, not a herpesvirus.
Azithromycin is used for pertussis, not for viral infections.
Clindamycin is added for toxin-mediated staphylococcal and streptococcal disease, not varicella.
explain.takeaway: Varicella (crops of papules, vesicles, and crusts in different stages, unlike smallpox and mpox) is treated with acyclovir or valacyclovir in patients ill enough to need therapy.
explain.topic: Severe varicella in an adolescent: antiviral therapy
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize varicella in an unvaccinated adolescent and choose its treatment (Case #5)

questions.stem:
A 15-year-old boy is admitted overnight with fever, chills, severe muscle pain, and a rash that went from macular to petechial to purpuric within hours. Spinal fluid shows a gram-negative diplococcus. The next morning his best friend, a teammate on his basketball team, comes to clinic. They shared water bottles at practice 2 days ago and rode home in the same car. The friend feels well and has a normal examination.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management for the friend?
choices: No action unless he develops a fever
Intravenous immunoglobulin as a single dose
Oral ciprofloxacin as soon as possible
Oral azithromycin for 5 days
A pneumococcal conjugate vaccine dose

explain.html: Neisseria meningitidis colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads through respiratory and throat secretions, and invasive disease can progress from fever and myalgia to petechiae, purpura, and shock within hours. The workshop case makes the point: a teenager with abrupt fever, chills, and severe myalgia develops skin lesions in the emergency department, and his best friend on the same team was admitted the night before with the same illness. Antimicrobial chemoprophylaxis is the primary way to prevent secondary cases of sporadic meningococcal disease. It goes to household members, child care contacts, and anyone directly exposed to the patient's oral secretions in the 7 days before symptom onset, given as soon as possible and ideally within 24 hours of identifying the index case, using rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone. This friend shared water bottles, so he qualifies, and waiting for fever would forfeit the window.
explain.table:
ExposureWho gets prophylaxisDrug
Invasive meningococcal diseaseHousehold, child care, anyone exposed to oral secretions in the 7 days before symptomsRifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone, ideally within 24 hours
Invasive Hib diseaseUnimmunized close contacts (household, day care)Rifampin for 4 days
PertussisAll family members and close contactsAzithromycin
why: Waiting for fever is too late, because invasive meningococcal disease can reach shock within hours.
Immunoglobulin is used in Kawasaki disease and streptococcal toxic shock, not for meningococcal exposure.
Azithromycin is the prophylaxis for pertussis contacts, not meningococcal contacts.
A pneumococcal vaccine does not protect against Neisseria meningitidis.
explain.takeaway: Close contacts of invasive meningococcal disease (household, child care, anyone exposed to oral secretions) receive chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone) as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

explain.objective: Recognize invasive meningococcal disease and manage its close contacts (Case #10)

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old boy had a sore throat, then 2 days of fever, vomiting, and severe left knee pain with a limp. In the emergency department his temperature is 40.0 C (104 F), pulse 183/min, and blood pressure 87/57 mm Hg. The knee is aspirated and the fluid is cloudy. A red rash spreads from his lower leg over his entire body, and he develops kidney and liver injury. Blood and joint fluid cultures grow beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains. He is taken for washout of the knee.

Clindamycin is added to his beta-lactam antibiotic mainly to accomplish which of the following?
choices: Cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in the joint
Neutralize toxin that is already circulating in the blood
Improve penetration of the antibiotic into spinal fluid
Prevent rheumatic fever after the throat infection
Stop the bacteria from making new superantigen toxin

explain.html: Group A streptococcal exotoxins act as superantigens, driving T cell proliferation and an overwhelming release of IL-1, IL-2, interferon gamma, and TNF-alpha that produces shock. The workshop case follows that path: a 5-year-old with a sore throat develops a septic knee, then high fever, tachycardia, falling blood pressure, a red rash spreading from the leg over the whole body, and multiorgan failure needing PICU care and surgical washout. Treatment has three parts, each aimed at a different target. The beta-lactam kills the organism, surgery removes the infected source, and a protein synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin is added because it stops the bacteria from making new toxin. Toxin that is already circulating cannot be reached by an antibiotic, so IVIG is added for the group A streptococcal form to neutralize it.
explain.table:
FeatureStaphylococcal TSSStreptococcal TSS
Typical settingMenstruation and tamponsSkin or joint infection, often after sore throat or a cut
ToxinTSST-1 (superantigen)Pyrogenic exotoxins A and B (superantigens)
BacteremiaLowCommon
AntibioticsAnti-staphylococcal plus a protein synthesis inhibitorAnti-streptococcal plus a protein synthesis inhibitor
Add-onSource removal (tampon)IVIG, surgical source control
why: The culture grows streptococci in chains, not staphylococci, so resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage is not the reason.
Neutralizing toxin already in the blood is the job of IVIG, not clindamycin.
Nothing suggests meningitis, and spinal fluid penetration is not why clindamycin is added.
Preventing rheumatic fever is not the goal during shock; stopping toxin production is.
explain.takeaway: In toxic shock syndrome a protein synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin) is added to stop superantigen production, and IVIG is added in the group A streptococcal form to neutralize circulating toxin.
explain.topic: Streptococcal toxic shock: why add a protein synthesis inhibitor
